content: The document outlines a comprehensive framework for managing lymphoedema and elephantiasis, focusing on community-based, health facility-based, and primary healthcare system approaches. 1. Management of Acute Attacks: The management of acute attacks in lymphatic filariasis (LF) is guided by an algorithm adapted from the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations. This involves identifying the severity of the condition and implementing appropriate interventions to prevent disability. 2. Home-Based Management of Lymphoedema: Three types of home-based care systems are recognized: Community or Family Home-Based Care: This involves training and monitoring by community or family members to support the patient. Health Facility-Based Care with Community Health Worker Support: This integrates care for lymphoedema with other chronic diseases like leprosy, diabetes, and neurological disorders. Primary Healthcare System: This incorporates disability prevention into the primary healthcare framework. 3. Selection of Management Systems: The choice of a management system depends on factors such as the number and distribution of patients, their social grouping, and community awareness and support. For example: If there are more than five cases of chronic lymphoedema or elephantiasis in a community, community home-based care is recommended. If there are fewer than five cases, family home-based, community home-based, or primary health center-based care can be considered. 4. Steps for Planning Home-Based Management: Determine the number and location of patients in the community. Engage the community and key figures to establish roles and responsibilities. Set up a follow-up system and select workers for involvement. Conduct monthly coordination meetings with medical staff and caregivers, establish a reporting system, and supervise technical and managerial issues. Register patients with community assistance. Estimate the required human resources, drugs, and supplies based on patient numbers and distribution. Organize training for community health workers and caregivers on home-based self-care principles, including hygiene, skin and wound care, limb elevation, exercises, and wearing comfortable shoes. 5. Training and Follow-Up: Train government and non-government health workers in lymphoedema management, emphasizing acute attack management. Establish a referral system for severe clinical manifestations. Conduct monthly visits to patients to provide education on disability prevention and involve relatives, friends, and neighbors in care. Organize regular supervision to ensure accurate data recording and maintain commitment to follow-up activities. 6. Community Morbidity Register: A community morbidity register is used to identify and track lymphoedema and hydrocele patients. This form helps health workers assess the severity of lymphoedema and document key demographic and clinical data. 7. Individual Intake and Follow-Up Forms: Health workers document patient demographics, the presence and location of swelling, lymphoedema staging, entry lesions, and acute attack history. Patients are trained in the five components of lymphoedema management: hygiene, skin and wound care, elevation, exercises, and wearing comfortable shoes. Danger signs such as chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, unexplained weight loss, jaundice, or rapid swelling onset indicate the need for immediate referral to a health facility. 8. Referral Criteria: Patients with scrotal swelling should be referred to a hospital for further evaluation and potential hydrocele surgery. Other reasons for referral include entry lesions with drainage, foul odor, redness, acute attacks, or psychological service needs. 9. Reporting Framework: Data flows from community health workers to the national program through health centers and implementation units. Reporting should be conducted at least annually and integrated with existing health information systems where feasible. 10. Sustainability and Monitoring: Regular refresher courses for those involved in lymphoedema management are recommended every two years. Data from follow-up forms allow tracking of patient progress and the number of visits during the reporting period. This framework ensures a structured and sustainable approach to managing lymphoedema and elephantiasis, emphasizing community involvement, regular monitoring, and integration with broader healthcare systems.
